title: Date, Time, and Timestamps with Time Zones
description: Master TIMESTAMPTZ vs TIMESTAMP, INTERVAL arithmetic, AT TIME ZONE conversion, and ISO 8601 formatting.

data.text: Handling timestamps correctly is essential for distributed applications. PostgreSQL provides two primary timestamp representations: **`TIMESTAMP WITHOUT TIME ZONE`** and **`TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE` (`TIMESTAMPTZ`)**.

When you store a value into `TIMESTAMPTZ`, PostgreSQL converts it from your client's local timezone into **UTC** and stores the UTC epoch physically in 8 bytes. When querying, it converts the UTC timestamp back to the requesting client's timezone setting. `TIMESTAMP WITHOUT TIME ZONE` completely discards timezone offsets, causing horrific bugs during Daylight Saving Time transitions!

data.title: Date Arithmetic with INTERVAL
data.code:
-- Adding intervals to current time
SELECT 
    NOW() AS current_time_utc,
    NOW() - INTERVAL '30 days' AS thirty_days_ago,
    NOW() + INTERVAL '2 hours 15 minutes' AS future_time,
    -- Converting timezone explicitly
    NOW() AT TIME ZONE 'America/New_York' AS new_york_time;

data.text: The One Sentence That Wins the Point

`TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE` does **not** store a time zone. It stores an absolute instant (microseconds since 2000-01-01 UTC) and displays it in the current session's `TimeZone` setting. `TIMESTAMP WITHOUT TIME ZONE` stores a wall-clock reading with no instant attached. That distinction explains every DST bug you will ever see.

data.title: How the Same Instant Looks in Different Time Zones
data.content: Set the session time zone and watch the same stored instant render differently.

data.title: The Daylight-Saving Gap
data.text: On 2026-03-08 in New York, 02:30 **does not exist** — the clock jumps from 02:00 to 03:00. A `TIMESTAMP` column holding that value silently refers to nothing, and arithmetic across the transition can be off by an hour. `TIMESTAMPTZ` has no such gap because it stores an instant.

data.title: Intervals, Truncation, and Buckets
data.content: Interval arithmetic is exact and reads well.
data.code:
SELECT now()                            AS now,
       now() - INTERVAL '30 days'         AS thirty_days_ago,
       now() + INTERVAL '2 hours 15 min'  AS later,
       date_trunc('month', now())          AS start_of_month,
       now() + INTERVAL '1 mon'            AS same_day_next_month;

-- Interval components
SELECT EXTRACT(epoch FROM INTERVAL '1 day 2 hours') AS seconds,   -- 93600
       EXTRACT(days  FROM INTERVAL '1 day 2 hours') AS days;      -- 1

-- Age between two timestamps as a human interval
SELECT age(now(), '1986-07-01'::date) AS postgres_age;

-- Grouping by day requires a stable bucket
SELECT date_trunc('day', happened) AS day, count(*)
FROM events
GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1;

data.text: `now()` and `CURRENT_TIMESTAMP` are the **transaction start time** and are identical; every row in a transaction sees the same value. `statement_timestamp()` is the statement start and `clock_timestamp()` advances during a statement. Use `now()` for `created_at`, and remember that long transactions stamp late rows with the transaction start time — a classic bug in batch letter generation.

data.title: Formatting, Parsing, and Ranges

rows: Imported wall-clock data, "local time at the store"
Opening hours (and even then, a zone is usually relevant)

data.title: Interview Answer
data.text: The rule to state: **store instants as `TIMESTAMPTZ`, render in the user's zone**. Filter ranges as half-open (`>= start AND < end`) so that midnight boundaries cannot double-count or drop rows.

data.title: Recreate a DST Bug and Fix It
steps: Create a `TIMESTAMP` column and insert `'2026-11-01 01:30'` twice, once before and once after the fall-back transition.
Order the rows and explain why they are ambiguous.
Rewrite the table using `TIMESTAMPTZ` and re-insert using explicit offsets.
Show that both rows are now distinguishable.
data.expectedOutcome: You can explain the DST ambiguity from a reproduction, not from memory.

items.question: Does `TIMESTAMPTZ` store the client time zone?
items.answer: No. It stores an instant and converts for display using the session `TimeZone`. Different clients see different local renderings of the same instant.

items.question: Should I store UTC strings or `TIMESTAMPTZ`?
items.answer: Use `TIMESTAMPTZ`. Storing text loses type safety, indexing semantics, and interval arithmetic, and invites mixed formats.

items.question: Why is `now()` the same for every row in a transaction?
items.answer: It returns the transaction timestamp so that a single statement sees a consistent time. Use `clock_timestamp()` if you truly need the wall clock, or `statement_timestamp()` per statement.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: PostgreSQL stores `TIMESTAMPTZ` in UTC internally and converts to client timezone dynamically.
Use `INTERVAL` for clean time addition and subtraction.
